The Russo-Ukrainian War has not only impacted military security but also environmental and scientific cooperation. The Arctic Council, a forum in which the United States and Russia had continued to collaborate despite the fallout over Russia’s Crimea annexation, paused its work shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. (Since Russia was chairing the Council at the time of the invasion, Member States and Permanent Participants refused to attend meetings in Russia.) The Arctic-7 continued to cooperate but in an alternate diplomatic arrangement rather than through the Council with Russia. At the time of this writing, the Norwegian Chairship (2023–2025) is supporting only Working Group projects in which Russia is not involved. Western sanctions have also complicated Western-Russian scientific collaboration on the Arctic’s most pressing problems. Owing to funding and data-sharing suspensions, Western scientists do not have access to the Russian Arctic, limiting research on climate change problems such as permafrost thaw (Konrad, 2023). Many scientists at the University of Alaska, a leader in the United States on Arctic research, are at a loss regarding how to continue their research collaborations with colleagues in Russia. The limited operational functioning of the Arctic Council and pan-Arctic scientific cooperation are jeopardizing our knowledge of climate change, already four times faster in the Arctic than the rest of the world (Rantanen et al., 2022).

The war has also impacted Alaska’s economy. Oil prices soared after Russia’s invasion until June 2022 before declining to roughly pre-war levels by the end of the year. Since approximately 44% of the State of Alaska’s revenue comes from petroleum (Alaska Department of Revenue, 2023),Footnote 5 the war-time price surge benefited Alaska’s economy significantly, although residents, like others elsewhere, paid higher gasoline prices.

. Alaska has received hundreds of Ukrainians since the outbreak of war (Maxwell, 2023). Their arrival has been significant enough to prompt the Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development to reopen its Office of Citizenship Assistance to assist refugees and immigrants in their search for employment in the state (Samuels, 2023). Meanwhile, as hundreds of thousands of Russians are fleeing military conscription, in October 2022 residents of Gambell on Alaska’s St. Lawrence Island in the north Bering Sea were shocked to encounter two Russian men arriving on a fishing boat from Chukotka in the hopes of dodging Russia’s draft and securing asylum (Grove, 2023). (Now settled in Tacoma, Washington, their plan succeeded.)

The Alaskan Territory was essential to the U.S. ability to transfer Lend-Lease military supplies during World War II from the continental United States to Siberia for Soviet defense. The military’s investment in Alaska in World War II provided a foundation to support the U.S. defense against the Soviets in the early Cold War. Following the polar concept, Alaska was at the frontlines of deterring, detecting, and stopping a Soviet attack. In turn, the people, infrastructure, and services the military brought to Alaska contributed to statehood in 1959. Alaska was a symbolic site of the melting of the Ice Curtain and one region in which the United States and Soviet Union could cooperate on environmental issues. . The Russo-Ukrainian War has ended most of the post-Cold War cooperation, in both bilateral and multilateral arrangements. The bifurcation of the Arctic impacts not only security but also collaboration on environmental issues and scientific research.

Alaska continues to play a part in U.S.–Russian relations, and the fallout between the two countries affects the state in a multitude of ways. After decades of declining U.S. attention to the Arctic and Alaska’s role in it, climate change and international relations after the Crimea annexation prompted the United States to elevate its position in the region. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 not only justified but accelerated the U.S. commitment to the North.
